panels.title: Latency — what a consumer actually waits for
Order latency — trade created to position computed
panels.description: How old a trade is when its position is computed. This is the pipeline's own work. What a consumer waits for is longer, because a record is not readable until the checkpoint that produced it commits.

panels.title: ③ p99
panels.description: Processing latency.

panels.title: ④ p99
panels.description: Processing latency.

options.content:
Add the checkpoint interval. A record is not readable until the checkpoint that produced it commits, so visible latency is roughly processing plus a uniform wait of up to one interval.

Measured: **p50 2.5s / max 5.0s** at a 5s interval, **p50 0.5s / max 1.0s** at 1s.

panels.title: Checkpoints — the floor under visible latency
panels.description: A record is not readable until the checkpoint that produced it commits, so the interval between these is what a consumer waits on top of the processing time. Duration is how long one takes and should stay far below the interval; it is on the left axis in milliseconds. The completed count is on the right, on its own scale -- sharing the millisecond axis made a count of 3000 render as '3 s' and read as duration climbing into seconds.

panels.title: last checkpoint
panels.description: How long the most recent checkpoint took.

panels.title: aborted checkpoints
panels.description: One per job is normal and happens at startup: with a short interval the first checkpoint triggers before every task is running and is aborted. A count that keeps climbing while the job runs is the thing to worry about; watch completed checkpoints rising alongside it.

options.content:
Visible latency is roughly processing plus a uniform wait of up to one checkpoint interval. Shorten the interval and the wait falls with it — at 1s the median order latency is about 0.5s.

A checkpoint takes about 13ms here, so it is the *interval* that costs, not the checkpoint.

panels.title: Saturation — is it keeping up, and if not, what is the ceiling
Consumer lag — records each source is behind
panels.description: How many records are sitting in Kafka that the job has not read yet. This is the signal that defines saturation: a bounded, sawtooth lag is a pipeline keeping up, and a line that climbs and never comes back down is one that is not, no matter how healthy throughput looks.

panels.title: ① orders lag
panels.description: Records waiting in the orders topic. Growing steadily means the offered load is above what this parallelism and core count can absorb.

options.content: Lag climbing? Find the task at 100% busy — that operator is the ceiling. The back-pressured tasks are everything queued behind it. If no single task stands out, the cluster is out of cores, not out of parallelism.

panels.title: Saturation — where the work is, and where it is stuck
panels.description: Busy is the share of each second a task spends doing work; back-pressured is the share it spends blocked because the task downstream of it cannot keep up. Busy near 100% with no back-pressure means the pipeline is working at its limit and keeping up. Sustained back-pressure means it is not: the offered load is above what this parallelism can absorb, and adding parallelism is what fixes it.

panels.title: busiest task
panels.description: Share of the second the hottest task spends working.

panels.title: back-pressure
panels.description: Sustained non-zero means the offered load exceeds this parallelism.

options.content: Offer more load than the job can take and back-pressure goes red while throughput flattens — that flat number is the ceiling for this parallelism. Double the parallelism and the ceiling should move, not the back-pressure.

panels.title: Where the work is — busy by task
panels.description: Share of each second every task spends doing work. One task near 100% while the rest sit low is a bottleneck, and it names the operator to fix: adding parallelism helps only the pinned one. Even bars mean the work is spread and the whole job is the constraint.

panels.title: Where it is stuck — back-pressure by task
panels.description: Share of each second every task spends blocked because the task downstream cannot keep up. Read it with the panel to the left: the back-pressured task is the victim, and the busy task it feeds is the cause.

panels.title: Resources — the ceilings underneath all of it
CPU — cores in use
panels.description: Derived from JVM CPU time, so it reads in cores rather than a percentage of an unstated whole and means the same thing on any machine. Compare it with the cores the host actually has -- and read it together with back-pressure before concluding anything: step 10 found the TaskManager at 3.85 of 8 cores while throughput was pinned, which looks like a CPU ceiling and was not one. Threads blocked waiting on Kafka acknowledgements are not busy, and they are not idle for want of work either.

panels.title: Heap — share of the limit
panels.description: Steady sawtooth is healthy. A floor that keeps rising means state is growing faster than it is being collected, and the job is heading for a GC spiral rather than an out-of-memory error — which is why this is worth watching next to the panel on the right.

panels.title: Garbage collection — pause per second
panels.description: Milliseconds of every second lost to GC. Tens of milliseconds is normal. Hundreds means the JVM is spending its time collecting instead of working, and it shows up as latency and back-pressure with no operator looking busy.

panels.title: Network — bytes moved per second
panels.description: Read from Kafka, written back to Kafka, and shuffled between subtasks. The account branch dominates: split_by_allocation fans each order into four allocations, so it carries four times the record rate and a matching share of the bytes. Compare against the link the deployment actually has.

panels.title: Network buffers — Flink's own back-pressure valve
panels.description: Back-pressure is not a policy, it is these buffers filling: a subtask that cannot hand its output on stops getting buffers and stops reading. Output pool usage climbing toward 100% is back-pressure forming, and it moves before latency does.

panels.title: free task slots
panels.description: Slots not currently held by a job. A submission with none free does not queue, it fails -- which is how a run once reported zero throughput while two dozen cancelled jobs sat holding the cluster.

panels.title: TaskManager threads
panels.description: Thread count rises with parallelism. On a fixed core count, more threads past the point of saturation buys context switching rather than throughput.

options.content:
Work down this row, but do not stop at the first plausible answer. **Cores** is the usual suspect and was the wrong one here: the TaskManager sat at 3.85 of 8 with throughput pinned, because its threads were blocked on Kafka rather than computing. Low CPU with high back-pressure means the constraint is downstream, not local.

**Heap and GC** is the quietest failure: latency and back-pressure rise with no operator looking busy. **Network** matters once bytes rather than records are the constraint. **Buffers** move first of all; they are the mechanism back-pressure is made of.

The broker is the blind spot -- Prometheus scrapes Flink only. It is also what actually capped this pipeline: one broker absorbs about 750k records/sec, and each order becomes five records, so ~137k orders/sec is the ceiling no parallelism can move.

panels.title: The broker — the ceiling step 10 ran into
Disk — log size per topic
panels.description: How much disk each topic holds. The account topic dominates, because every order becomes four allocations there against one position on the symbol side -- the same four-to-one that makes the write path the ceiling shows up here as four-to-one on disk.

panels.title: Broker — bytes in and out
panels.description: What the broker is actually absorbing and serving, measured at the broker rather than inferred from the job. Compare with the Flink network panel above: they should agree, and when they do not, something else is talking to this cluster.

panels.title: Broker — capacity left
panels.description: The share of the time the broker's request handlers are idle, in its own words rather than inferred from back-pressure upstream. Falling toward zero is the broker saying it is the bottleneck. Step 10 spent a long time establishing that by elimination; this panel answers it directly.

panels.title: Broker — produce request time
panels.description: How long a produce request takes and where it goes. Queue time rising while local time stays flat means the broker is saturated rather than slow.

panels.title: broker CPU cores
panels.description: Read against the host's core count and the TaskManager's usage: on one machine they are spending the same eight.

panels.title: broker heap
panels.description: The broker's own heap. Its page cache matters more than its heap for write speed, and neither is visible from Flink's metrics.

panels.title: Why the broker is on this dashboard

options.content:
It was left off deliberately at first: the dashboard is about what the pipeline produced, not the plumbing. Step 10 changed that. One broker absorbs about **750,000 records/sec**, each order becomes five records, and the pipeline pins at ~150,000 orders/sec under every parallelism, partition count and core budget tried.

That took a week of `docker stats` and elimination to establish. **Capacity left** answers it in one panel.
